::: {.callout-note title="Goals for this chapter"}
- Name the two functions of the lungs, oxygenation and ventilation, and say why the course studies them separately before putting them back together.
- Describe how a breath happens in one sentence: the muscles lower pleural pressure, air flows in, and relaxation lets it flow out.
- Name the parts of the respiratory system (lungs, chest wall including the diaphragm, pleural space, airways, muscles) and the three places a problem can sit: lung, chest wall or muscles.
- Place each lecture of the block on the path of O~2~ from the air to the tissues and of CO~2~ back out.
- Recognize the two frameworks the block uses for a low PaO~2~ (the A–a gradient) and a high PaCO~2~ (a balance of strength and load). Later lectures teach both.

This chapter is a preview. Everything in it comes back in more detail later in the block.
:::

The respiratory block opens with a short tour. The point of the tour is a framework: when the details of pressures, partial pressures and dissociation curves start to pile up, you should be able to say which part of the system you are in and which of the two jobs it serves. This chapter covers that tour. The next one, [Respiratory Statics](statics.qmd), starts the details.

## Breathe in, breathe out

Take a deep breath in, then let it out. To breathe in, you used your muscles, mostly the diaphragm, to make the chest bigger. That lowered the pressure around the lungs, the lungs expanded, and air was sucked in through the open airway. To breathe out, you did nothing. You relaxed, and the system sprang back to where it rests. You can also breathe out forcibly, using expiratory muscles, but quiet breathing spends all of its energy on inspiration.

That is most of respiratory mechanics in two sentences. We are negative-pressure breathers: we pull air in by lowering the pressure around the lungs, not by pushing it in. Keep that picture in mind when the pressure symbols multiply in the statics and dynamics chapters.

## Why we need lungs at all

A single cell living in water gets its O~2~ by diffusion. Outside the cell, O~2~ is high and CO~2~ is low. Inside, the mitochondria use O~2~ and make CO~2~. Each gas moves down its gradient across the membrane, and nothing else is needed (@fig-respiratory-intro-circuit A).

![Why a multicellular body needs lungs and a circulation. (A) A single cell exchanges O~2~ and CO~2~ with its surroundings by diffusion alone. (B) In the body, ventilation brings fresh air to the alveoli and removes CO~2~, gas diffuses between the alveoli and the blood, and the circulation carries O~2~ to the tissues and CO~2~ back to the lungs. Course figure.](figures/respiratory-intro/circuit.svg){#fig-respiratory-intro-circuit}

A cell in your kidney or your calf muscle is far from fresh air, so the body does the same job in stages (@fig-respiratory-intro-circuit B). Bulk flow of air (ventilation) brings air rich in O~2~ to the alveoli. O~2~ diffuses across the thin alveolar-capillary barrier into the blood and binds to hemoglobin. The circulation carries it to the tissues, where it diffuses out to the cells that use it. CO~2~ makes the reverse trip, and the same bulk flow of air blows it off. The intent in the mitochondria is the same as in the single cell. The body just needs several organs to keep the gradients in place.

The cardiovascular block ended with the blood going round and round. This block assumes that and asks how the lungs load O~2~ into that blood and take CO~2~ out of it.

## Two jobs: oxygenation and ventilation

The lungs do two things.

- **Oxygenation** is getting O~2~ from the air into the arterial blood. Its end point is the arterial PO~2~ (PaO~2~) and the saturation of hemoglobin.
- **Ventilation** is getting CO~2~ out of the body. Its end point is the arterial PCO~2~ (PaCO~2~).

Both happen in the same lungs with the same breaths, but what controls each one is different, so the course teaches them as if they were in separate silos. Once you know how each works, the later lectures put them back together and ask how a problem with one affects the other. When you meet a patient who is short of breath, the first question the course teaches you to ask is: is this a problem of oxygenation, of ventilation, or both?

## The parts of the system

The respiratory system has these parts:

- **The lungs**: the airways, which conduct air, and the alveoli, where gas exchange happens.
- **The chest wall**: the ribs, the intercostal muscles, and everything else that surrounds the thorax. The diaphragm counts as part of the chest wall. It forms the floor of the thorax, and it is also the main muscle of inspiration. It does most of the work in quiet breathing, with help from the intercostal and scalene muscles, and more neck muscles join in when you breathe hard.
- **The pleural space**: the thin, closed space between the lungs and the chest wall. It holds almost no fluid, and because it is sealed, it links the two. When the chest wall is pulled outward, pleural pressure falls, the lungs are pulled outward with it, alveolar pressure falls below the pressure at the mouth, and air rushes in.

The course compresses the mechanics into one phrase: **the chest wall wants to be big, and the lungs want to be small.** Linked by the pleural space, they settle at a volume where the two pulls balance. That resting volume, at the end of a quiet breath out, is the functional residual capacity (FRC). The lecture calls FRC the starting point of respiratory physiology, the way mean systemic filling pressure (P~ms~) was the starting point of the circulation's Guyton curves.

Because the system has three parts, a problem can sit in only three places: **the lung, the chest wall, or the muscles.** The course uses that idea all through the block, from the pressure-volume curves of statics to the pulmonary function tests at the end.

## A map of the block

@fig-respiratory-intro-block-map lays the lectures along the path that O~2~ takes. Each box is one or more chapters of this book.

![The pulmonary block as a path from the air to the mitochondria. Mechanics moves the air, ventilation sets the gas in the alveoli, gas exchange moves it into the blood, and transport carries it to the tissues. Control of ventilation sits underneath and adjusts the whole chain. Course figure.](figures/respiratory-intro/block-map.svg){#fig-respiratory-intro-block-map}

**Mechanics.** [Respiratory Statics](statics.qmd) names the lung volumes and capacities and explains the pressure-volume curves of the lung, the chest wall and the whole respiratory system, and how the muscles set the largest and smallest volumes. [Respiratory Dynamics I](dynamics-1.qmd) makes the system move: how pleural pressure, alveolar pressure and flow change through one quiet breath. [Respiratory Dynamics II](dynamics-2.qmd) adds the airways. Ohm's law returns from the cardiovascular block (pressure difference = flow × resistance), and airway resistance is what goes wrong in common diseases such as asthma. It also explains why even healthy people hit a limit on how fast they can breathe out.

**Ventilation.** [Alveolar Ventilation](ventilation.qmd) follows air from the atmosphere to the alveoli. Minute ventilation is tidal volume times breathing rate (V̇~E~ = V~T~ × RR), much as cardiac output is stroke volume times heart rate. Part of each breath only fills the conducting airways, so it is alveolar ventilation (V̇~A~) that matters. The alveolar gas equation gives the alveolar PO~2~, and V̇~A~ sets the PaCO~2~.

**Gas exchange.** [Diffusion](diffusion.qmd) covers how gas crosses the alveolar-capillary barrier, written as Fick's law of diffusion. [Ventilation and Perfusion](ventilation-perfusion.qmd) covers the matching of air to blood. Where there is a lot of blood flow there should be a lot of ventilation. A unit with blood flow but no air (shunt) or air but no blood flow (dead space) wastes effort.

**Transport.** [Transport of O~2~ and CO~2~](o2-co2-transport.qmd) covers hemoglobin, O~2~ content, and the Fick principle, V̇O~2~ = Q̇ × (CaO~2~ − CvO~2~). O~2~ delivery is cardiac output times arterial O~2~ content. [Pulmonary Acid Base](acid-base.qmd) adds the link between CO~2~ and pH.

**Control.** [Control of Ventilation](control-of-ventilation.qmd) covers how the brainstem senses CO~2~, pH and O~2~ and adjusts breathing, mostly without your noticing. Ask someone to think about their breathing and it gets messed up.

**Putting it together.** [Physiology of Exercise](exercise.qmd) revisits exercise from the respiratory side: if cardiac output rises several-fold, the same extra blood flows through the lungs, and ventilation has to keep up. [Think Like a Respiratory Consultant](respiratory-consultant.qmd) brings the whole block to the patient through pulmonary function testing. The pulmonary circulation was taught in the cardiovascular block; see [Pulmonary Circulation](../cardiovascular/pulmonary-circulation.qmd).

The tour also named the lung volumes and capacities (tidal volume, FRC, TLC, RV, vital capacity); [Respiratory Statics](statics.qmd) defines them.

Pulmonary function tests run through the whole block. A full set is spirometry, lung volumes from a body box, and the diffusing capacity. This is not the clinical part of the curriculum, but disease is a useful counterexample: seeing how emphysema or interstitial lung disease breaks the normal physiology makes the normal physiology clearer. The course uses those diseases as labels for physiological patterns, not to teach their treatment.

::: {.callout-tip title="How to work in this block"}
The lecture compares respiratory physiology to the game Othello: a minute to learn, a lifetime to master. There are not that many facts, but they combine in many ways. Work with a pencil. Most of the graphs in this block are curves that bend, and you learn them by drawing them, moving them, and drawing them again.
:::

## Two scaffolds you will fill in

Two frameworks organize the clinical end of the block. This section is a preview: the hypoxemia framework is taught in [Ventilation and Perfusion](ventilation-perfusion.qmd), and the hypercapnia framework in [Pulmonary Acid Base](acid-base.qmd) and [Think Like a Respiratory Consultant](respiratory-consultant.qmd). It helps to see their shape now (@fig-respiratory-intro-scaffolds).

![The two frameworks of the block. (A) Hypoxemia, sorted by the A–a gradient into causes that lower alveolar PO~2~ and causes that impair gas exchange. (B) Hypercapnia, a ventilation problem, as an imbalance between the strength of the respiratory system and the load it has to move. Course figure.](figures/respiratory-intro/scaffolds.svg){#fig-respiratory-intro-scaffolds}

### Oxygenation: why is the PaO~2~ low?

*Hypoxemia* means a low PaO~2~. To work out why, the course starts from the alveolar gas equation, which gives the PO~2~ in the alveoli:

$$P_AO_2 = (P_B - P_{H_2O})\,F_iO_2 - \frac{P_aCO_2}{R}$$

Here P~B~ is barometric pressure, P~H2O~ is water vapor pressure (47 mm Hg), FiO~2~ is the fraction of O~2~ in inspired air (0.21 for room air), and R is the respiratory exchange ratio (about 0.8). The [Alveolar Ventilation](ventilation.qmd) chapter derives it.

If you know the PAO~2~ and measure the PaO~2~, the difference between them is the **A–a gradient** (PAO~2~ − PaO~2~). It sorts hypoxemia into two groups.

- **A–a gradient normal: the alveolar PO~2~ itself is low.** Either barometric pressure is low (high altitude), the inspired O~2~ fraction is low (for example, a confined space where another gas has displaced O~2~), or the patient is hypoventilating, so CO~2~ builds up in the alveoli and takes the place of O~2~ (a high PaCO~2~ in the equation). The lungs pass on what they receive, and what they receive is too little.
- **A–a gradient raised: the alveolar gas is fine, but O~2~ is not getting into the blood.** The causes are diffusion limitation, ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch and shunt.

A low O~2~ content in mixed venous blood, as in heart failure or fever, makes each of these gas-exchange problems worse, because the blood that escapes full exchange arrives with less O~2~ to begin with. In normal lungs it causes almost no hypoxemia on its own.

Later lectures add a second branch point: does the PaO~2~ rise with supplemental O~2~? Hypoxemia from V/Q mismatch or diffusion limitation improves. Hypoxemia from shunt responds poorly, because the shunted blood never meets the extra O~2~.

::: {.callout-note title="If you are comparing with the slides"}
The Intro hypoxemia slide lists "Poor venous saturation/admixture" as a fourth cause of a raised PAO~2~ − PaO~2~. A low mixed venous saturation lowers PaO~2~ only through blood that passes a shunt, low V/Q units, or a diffusion-limited barrier. It makes those three mechanisms worse rather than standing as a mechanism of its own, which is how the Ventilation and Perfusion lecture presents its shunt case. The course errata make the same correction.
:::

### Ventilation: why is the PaCO~2~ high?

*Hypercapnia* means a high PaCO~2~. The PaCO~2~ is set by how fast CO~2~ is made and how fast alveolar ventilation clears it:

$$P_aCO_2 \propto \frac{\dot{V}CO_2}{\dot{V}_A}$$

A high PaCO~2~ almost always means the alveolar ventilation is too low for the CO~2~ being made. The course asks why with a balance. On one side is the strength of the system: the drive from the brainstem, the nerves and the respiratory muscles. On the other is the load: stiff lungs, narrowed airways, a heavy or stiff chest wall, or a large amount of CO~2~ to clear. When the load outweighs the strength, ventilation falls behind. The course's shorthand is "won't breathe" (drive is low, as with opioids) versus "can't breathe" (the muscles cannot move the load). [Pulmonary Acid Base](acid-base.qmd) and [Think Like a Respiratory Consultant](respiratory-consultant.qmd) work through it.

## Check your understanding

1. You hold your breath at the end of a quiet exhalation and relax every muscle. Why does your chest neither shrink nor expand?

    <details><summary>Answer</summary>

    You are at FRC. The lungs pull inward and the chest wall pulls outward, and at this volume the two pulls are equal, so no muscle force is needed to hold it. The pleural space links them, so they must share one volume.

    </details>

2. Which of the two lung functions does each of these measure: the PaCO~2~, the PaO~2~, the hemoglobin saturation?

    <details><summary>Answer</summary>

    PaCO~2~ measures ventilation. PaO~2~ and saturation measure oxygenation. A patient can have a problem with one and not the other, which is why the course asks "oxygenation or ventilation?" first.

    </details>

3. A climber on a high mountain has a low PaO~2~. Her lungs are healthy. Would you expect her A–a gradient to be normal or raised, and why?

    <details><summary>Answer</summary>

    Normal. Barometric pressure is low, so the alveolar PO~2~ is low, and healthy lungs pass that low PO~2~ on to the blood. The gradient between alveolus and artery is not the problem; the alveolar PO~2~ is.

    </details>

4. A patient breathes in normally but cannot breathe out forcibly. Can she still exhale a quiet tidal breath? Why?

    <details><summary>Answer</summary>

    Yes. Quiet expiration is passive. When the inspiratory muscles relax, the respiratory system's net inward recoil above FRC (the lungs' inward pull now exceeds the chest wall's outward pull) pushes the air back out and returns the system to FRC. Expiratory muscles are only needed to breathe out below FRC or faster than recoil alone allows.

    </details>

5. You are handed four numbers for a patient: SaO~2~, PaCO~2~, FEV~1~ and PaO~2~. Which would you look at to decide whether the problem is one of oxygenation or of ventilation, and which job does each report on?

    <details><summary>Answer</summary>

    PaO~2~ and SaO~2~ report on oxygenation, and PaCO~2~ reports on ventilation, so those three answer the question. FEV~1~ reports on neither directly. It measures how fast air can be blown out of the lungs, which is mechanics: a low FEV~1~ can lead to a ventilation or an oxygenation problem, or to neither.

    </details>

## Equations you will meet in this block

| Equation | Use | Taught in |
|---|---|---|
| ΔP = flow × resistance | Ohm's law, for air as for blood | [Respiratory Dynamics I](dynamics-1.qmd) and [II](dynamics-2.qmd) |
| V̇~E~ = V~T~ × RR | Minute ventilation | [Alveolar Ventilation](ventilation.qmd) |
| PAO~2~ = (P~B~ − P~H2O~) FiO~2~ − PaCO~2~/R | Alveolar gas equation | [Alveolar Ventilation](ventilation.qmd) |
| A–a gradient = PAO~2~ − PaO~2~ | Sorting hypoxemia | [Ventilation and Perfusion](ventilation-perfusion.qmd) |
| PaCO~2~ ∝ V̇CO~2~ / V̇~A~ | Ventilation and CO~2~ | [Alveolar Ventilation](ventilation.qmd) |
| V̇O~2~ = Q̇ × (CaO~2~ − CvO~2~) | Fick principle | [Transport of O~2~ and CO~2~](o2-co2-transport.qmd) |
| O~2~ delivery = Q̇ × CaO~2~ | Delivery to the tissues | [Transport of O~2~ and CO~2~](o2-co2-transport.qmd) |
